profile.title: Gradient-boosted river and rainfall forecasts with impact modeling and Sentinel‑1 flood mapping for Assam
profile.one_line: A combined river‑flow, rainfall, and satellite‑based system predicts short‑term floods, affected districts, and current flood extents in Assam, India.
profile.problem: Accurate short‑term flood forecasting and real‑time flood extent mapping in data‑sparse, monsoon‑affected river basins such as the Brahmaputra in Assam.
profile.setting: Monsoon season (May‑October) in Assam, India, using historical river discharge (GloFAS 1997‑2020), daily rainfall (NASA POWER 1997‑2026), district‑level impact reports from ASDMA (2021‑2026), and Sentinel‑1 radar imagery (Sen1Floods11).
data: Daily river discharge at 12 stations (GloFAS v4) 1997‑2026
Daily rainfall at 15 catchment points (NASA POWER) 1997‑2026
Sentinel‑1 VV/VH radar scenes from Sen1Floods11 (10 countries, including Assam)
methods: LightGBM gradient‑boosted models per lead time (1‑7 days) using lagged flow and multi‑scale rainfall features to predict river‑level exceedance
Logistic‑regression impact model that combines river forecasts, district rainfall, and historical district flood records to predict ASDMA‑reported affected populations
U‑Net with ResNet‑18 encoder trained from scratch on Sentinel‑1 data to segment flood water masks
baselines: Otsu thresholding for flood mask segmentation
profile.evaluation: Critical Success Index (CSI) for river flood warnings, day‑by‑day early‑warning performance against ASDMA 2022 reports, district‑month impact CSI (2021‑2026), and Water IoU and pixel accuracy for satellite flood masks (Sen1Floods11 test set).
contributions: A walk‑forward backtested gradient‑boosted river‑flow and rainfall model achieving CSI up to 0.82 for 1‑day forecasts in Assam.
An impact model that directly predicts district‑level reported flood impacts, improving CSI to 0.41 compared to river‑only and historical baselines.
A U‑Net flood‑water segmentation model attaining 0.72 Water IoU on Assam scenes, substantially outperforming an Otsu threshold baseline.
limitations: River flow input is a reanalysis product (GloFAS) rather than in‑situ gauge measurements.
Rainfall is sampled at only 15 points, limiting capture of highly localized downpours.
ASDMA impact data are limited to 2021‑2026 and are monthly, with daily detail available for only one year.
District‑to‑station matching relies on nearest‑station assignment with manual adjustments.
profile.research_question: What are effective data‑driven approaches for short‑term river flood forecasting, impact prediction, and satellite‑based flood extent mapping in monsoon‑affected basins with limited ground observations?

facts.text: code (floodwatch/forecast.py): Flood forecasting for Assam's rivers, 1-7 days ahead, with honest walk-forward backtesting.

code (floodwatch/forecast.py): Data: daily river discharge (GloFAS v4 via Open-Meteo, 1997-2026) at 12 river stations: six on the Brahmaputra main stem from Dibrugarh to Dhubri, plus the Subansiri, Jia Bharali, Dhansiri, Kopili, Beki/Manas and Barak.

code (floodwatch/forecast.py): Flood definition: flow above the station's 2-year return-period level, the standard "flood alert" threshold used by GloFAS. It is computed from the annual maxima of the TRAINING years only, so the test never leaks.

code (floodwatch/forecast.py): Why it can see the future: water takes days to travel down the Brahmaputra. A surge passing Dibrugarh today reaches Guwahati around 3 days later, so upstream stations are informative features for downstream forecasts.
code (floodwatch/forecast.py): Backtest: expanding-window walk-forward. To forecast year Y, the model is trained only on 1997..Y-1. Test years: 2021-2026.
code (floodwatch/impact.py): Impact-based flood forecasting: predict where ASDMA will REPORT people affected, not just where a river crosses a line.
code (floodwatch/impact.py): Unit: district-month in the monsoon (May-Oct), 2021-2026, 33 districts. Target: ASDMA reported >= MIN_AFFECTED people affected in that district-month.

code (floodwatch/impact.py): Features (all available before the month's impacts are known): * the river forecast signals for the district's station, taken from the walk-forward backtest (so they are genuinely out-of-sample): max forecast probability at each lead, days warned, days above warning level, peak flow relative to warning level * the same signals for the station upstream on the Brahmaputra * the district's flood history from OTHER years only (exposure / vulnerability) * month of the year
code (floodwatch/impact.py): Evaluation: leave-one-year-out. For each year 2021-2026, train on the other five years, tune the alert cut-off inside those five, predict the held-out year.
code (floodwatch/segment.py): Flood mapping from Sentinel-1 radar (VV, VH) with a U-Net.

code (floodwatch/segment.py): Radar sees through monsoon cloud, which is why agencies map floods with it. Calm water reflects the radar pulse away from the satellite, so it shows up dark; the hard cases are wet soil, shadows and urban areas.
code (floodwatch/segment.py): Data: Sen1Floods11 hand-labelled chips (446 scenes, 11 flood events incl. Assam). Baseline: Otsu thresholding on VH, the classic operational method.
code (floodwatch/validate_asdma.py): Validate forecasts against REAL flood impacts: ASDMA's district reports.

code (floodwatch/validate_asdma.py): Ground truth: population reported affected by floods, per district and month (ASDMA FRIMS reports, compiled by CivicDataLab's IDS-DRR project), Apr 2021 - Sep 2026.
code (floodwatch/validate_asdma.py): Unit of evaluation: district-month in the monsoon (May-Oct). A district-month counts as "flooded" when ASDMA reported at least MIN_AFFECTED people affected.
code (floodwatch/validate_asdma.py): A forecast "warned" that district-month if, on any day of the month, the 3-day forecast for the district's river station crossed its alert cut-off.

code (floodwatch/validate_asdma.py): Baselines: climatology flag every June and July (the usual peak months) river_above the river was actually above warning level that month: an observation, not a forecast, so a ceiling for river-only methods
code (floodwatch/validate_daily.py): Day-by-day check against ASDMA's daily district reports for the 2022 monsoon.

code (floodwatch/validate_daily.py): Truth: a district is "flooded" on a day when ASDMA reported >= MIN_AFFECTED people affected. Question: when a district's flooding STARTS (first flooded day after a quiet week), had the forecast for its river station warned 1, 3 and 5 days before?

code (floodwatch/validate_daily.py): Compared: the river-only model, the river + rainfall model, and two simple references: rain_only heavy local rain in the past 3 days (top 10% of 3-day totals at the nearest rain point) near_level river already above 85% of its warning level Data: 2022 daily FRIMS reports as compiled by CivicDataLab (data/asdma/daily_2022.csv).
code (scripts/export_site.py): Export the real model outputs the website shows (all from the backtest; nothing invented).

code (scripts/fetch_rain.py): Daily rainfall 1997-2026 at catchment points from NASA POWER (MERRA-2 / IMERG-based PRECTOTCORR, mm/day). Upstream Arunachal / Bhutan / Meghalaya rain reaches Assam's rivers days later; local rain drives floods the main-river gauges miss.

code (scripts/find_gauges.py): Snap each named river station to the GloFAS grid cell carrying the main channel (the cell with the highest flow in a small neighbourhood), then save its full daily history.
code (scripts/live_forecast.py): Daily live forecast: fetch the latest river flow, forecast 1-7 days ahead, write docs/data/live.json.
code (scripts/live_forecast.py): Runs every morning on GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/daily.yml). Uses only flow observed up to today, the same inputs the backtested model saw.
code (scripts/wayback_scan.py): Find which daily ASDMA flood reports (2015-2020, Jun-Oct) the Internet Archive saved.

Flood forecasting and satellite flood mapping for Assam, India, tested on six real monsoons (2021–2026) against river data and against the Assam State Disaster Management Authority's (ASDMA) district flood reports.

Live site: https://samiyakazi23.github.io/floodwatch/ · today's forecast (updated every morning), a live river dashboard, and a date checker that compares any day's forecast from 2021 to 2026 with what actually happened.
1. Will the rivers flood in the next 1–7 days? A gradient-boosted model reads daily flow at 12 river stations and rainfall at 15 points across the basin, and learns how surges travel down the valley.
2. Will people actually be affected, and where? An impact model turns river forecasts, local rainfall and district history into the chance that ASDMA reports people affected.
3. Where is the water right now? A U-Net maps floodwater from Sentinel-1 radar, which sees through monsoon cloud.

cards.title: Flood Prediction Using Machine Learning Models: Literature Review
cards.abstract: Floods are among the most destructive natural disasters, which are highly complex to model. The research on the advancement of flood prediction models has been contributing to risk reduction, policy suggestion, minimizing loss of human life and reducing the property damage associated with floods. To mimic the complex mathematical expressions of physical processes of floods, during the past two decades, machine learning (ML) methods have highly contributed in the advancement of prediction systems providing better performance and cost effective solutions. Due to the vast benefits and potential of ML, its popularity has dramatically increased among hydrologists. Researchers through introducing the novel ML methods and hybridization of the existing ones have been aiming at discovering more accurate and efficient prediction models. The main contribution is to demonstrate the state of the art of ML models in flood prediction and give an insight over the most suitable models. The literature where ML models are benchmarked through a qualitative analysis of robustness, accuracy, effectiveness, and speed have been particularly investigated to provide an extensive overview on various ML algorithms usage in the field. The performance comparison of ML models presents an in-depth understanding about the different techniques within the framework of a comprehensive evaluation and discussion. As the result, the paper introduces the most promising prediction methods for both long-term and short-term floods. Furthermore, the major trends in improving the quality of the flood prediction models are investigated. Among them, hybridization, data decomposition, algorithm ensemble, and model optimization are reported the most effective strategy in improvement of the ML methods. This survey can be used as a guideline for the hydrologists as well as climate scientists to assist them choosing the proper ML method according to the prediction task conclusions.

cards.title: A review on the applications of machine learning for runoff modeling
cards.abstract: Abstract The growing menace of global warming and restrictions on access to water in each region is a huge threat to global hydrological sustainability. Hence, the perspective at which hydrological studies are currently being carried out across the world to quantify and understand the water cycle modeling requires a further boost. In the past few decades, the theoretical understanding of machine learning (ML) algorithms for solving engineering issues, and the application of this method to practical problems have made very significant progress. In the field of hydrology, ML has been using for a better understanding of hydrological complexities. Then, using ML-based approaches for hydrological simulation have been a popular method for runoff modeling in recent years; it seems necessary to understand the application of ML in runoff modeling fully. Current research seeks to have an overview for rainfall–runoff modeling using ML approaches in recent years, including integrated and ordinary ML techniques (such as ANFIS, ANN, and SVM models). The main hydrological topics in this review study include surface hydrology, streamflow, rainfall–runoff, and flood modeling via ML approaches. Therefore, in this study, the author has critically reviewed the characteristics of machine learning models in runoff simulation, including advantages and disadvantages of three widely used machine learning models.

cards.title: A Review of Hydrodynamic and Machine Learning Approaches for Flood Inundation Modeling
cards.abstract: Machine learning (also called data-driven) methods have become popular in modeling flood inundations across river basins. Among data-driven methods, traditional machine learning (ML) approaches are widely used to model flood events, and recently deep learning (DL) approaches have gained more attention across the world. In this paper, we reviewed recently published literature on ML and DL applications for flood modeling for various hydrologic and catchment characteristics. Our extensive literature review shows that DL models produce better accuracy compared to traditional approaches. Unlike physically based models, ML/DL models suffer from the lack of using expert knowledge in modeling flood events. Apart from challenges in implementing a uniform modeling approach across river basins, the lack of benchmark data to evaluate model performance is a limiting factor for developing efficient ML/DL models for flood inundation modeling.

cards.title: Flood Forecasting with Machine Learning Technique on Hydrological Modeling
cards.abstract: Urban flooding is a major problem in Thailand. An essential countermeasure towards better flooding management is to forecast flood water levels in the real-time manner. Most existing early warning systems (EWS) in Thailand contain a lot of miscalculations when they face with real situations. Towards prediction improvement, this paper presents hydrological modeling augmented with alternative five machine learning techniques; linear regression, neural network regression, Bayesian linear regression and boosted decision tree regression. As the testbed system, the so-called MIKE-11 hydrologic forecasting model, developed by Danish Hydraulic Institute (DHI), Denmark, is used. To test error reduction in runoff forecasting, the water-level records during 2012-2016 data are used for training and the derived model is tested on the record of 2017, in the experiments.

cards.title: Machine learning applications in flood forecasting and predictions, challenges, and way-out in the perspective of changing environment
cards.abstract: Floods have been identified as one of the world's most common and widely distributed natural disasters over the last few decades. Floods' negative impacts could be significantly reduced if accurately predicted or forecasted in advance. Apart from large-scale spatiotemporal data and greater attention to data from the Internet of Things, the worldwide volume of digital data is increasing. Artificial intelligence plays a vital role in analyzing and developing the corresponding flood mitigation plan, flood prediction, or forecast. Machine learning (ML)-based models have recently received much attention due to their self-learning capabilities from data without incorporating any complex physical processes. This study provides a comprehensive review of ML approaches used in flood prediction, forecasting, and classification tasks, serving as a guide for future challenges. The importance and challenges of applying these techniques to flood prediction are discussed. Finally, recommendations and future directions of ML models in flood analysis are presented.

cards.title: Hybrid machine learning hydrological model for flood forecast purpose
cards.abstract: Abstract Machine learning-based data-driven models have achieved great success since their invention. Nowadays, the artificial neural network (ANN)-based machine learning methods have made great progress than ever before, such as the deep learning and reinforcement learning, etc. In this study, we coupled the ANN with the K-nearest neighbor method to propose a novel hybrid machine learning (HML) hydrological model for flood forecast purpose. The advantage of the proposed model over traditional neural network models is that it can predict discharge continuously without accuracy loss owed to its specially designed model structure. In order to overcome the local minimum issue of the traditional neural network training, a genetic algorithm and Levenberg–Marquardt-based multi-objective training method was also proposed. Real-world applications of the HML hydrological model indicated its satisfactory performance and reliable stability, which enlightened the possibility of further applications of the HML hydrological model in flood forecast problems.

cards.title: Flood Prediction using Hydrologic and ML-based Modeling: A Systematic Review
cards.abstract: Flooding, caused by the overflow of water bodies beyond their natural boundaries, has severe environmental and socioeconomic consequences. To effectively predict and mitigate flood events, accurate and reliable flood modeling techniques are essential. This study provides a comprehensive review of the latest modeling techniques used in flood prediction, classifying them into two main categories: hydrologic models and machine learning models based on artificial intelligence. By objectively assessing the advantages and disadvantages of each model type, we aim to synthesize a systematic analysis of the various flood modeling approaches in the current literature. Additionally, we explore the potential of hybrid strategies that combine both modeling methods' best characteristics to develop more effective flood control measures. Our findings provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners in the field of flood modeling, and our recommendations can contribute to the development of more efficient and accurate flood prediction systems.

cards.title: ML for Flood Forecasting at Scale
cards.abstract: Effective riverine flood forecasting at scale is hindered by a multitude of factors, most notably the need to rely on human calibration in current methodology, the limited amount of data for a specific location, and the computational difficulty of building continent/global level models that are sufficiently accurate. Machine learning (ML) is primed to be useful in this scenario: learned models often surpass human experts in complex high-dimensional scenarios, and the framework of transfer or multitask learning is an appealing solution for leveraging local signals to achieve improved global performance. We propose to build on these strengths and develop ML systems for timely and accurate riverine flood prediction.

cards.title: Machine learning-based hydrological models for flash floods: a systematic literature review
cards.abstract: Abstract Flash floods are critical events for emergency management, yet their modeling remains highly challenging, even in smart cities approaches. Physically based hydrological models are often unsuitable at small spatiotemporal scales due to their computational complexity and dependence on detailed local parameters, which are rarely available during flash floods. With the growing availability of hydrological data, machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising alternative. This work performs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to improve our understanding of the research landscape on ML applications for flash flood forecasting, a significant subset of flash flood modeling. From more than 1,200 papers published until January 2024 in Web of Science, SCOPUS/Elsevier, Springer/Nature, and Wiley, 50 were selected following PRISMA guidelines. The inclusion and exclusion criteria removed reviews, retractions, papers focused on post-flood damage assessment (not forecasting), and those with time resolutions of 6 hours or more, retaining only studies with fine-scale temporal data (<6 hours). For each paper, we extracted information on forecasting horizon, study area size, input data, ML techniques, and outcomes (regression or classification). Results show a sharp rise in ML-based flash flood research, with China leading (38%). Nearly all studies rely on rainfall, discharge, and water level data - often in combination. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks dominate (60%). Unfortunately, only 10% of the selected studies provide access to their datasets. This lack of transparency poses a major barrier to reproducibility, inhibits fair comparative evaluation of models, and ultimately slows methodological progress in flash flood forecasting. Furthermore, our review highlights that no method consistently outperforms others. This variability in performance is likely influenced by factors such as regional hydrological characteristics (e.g., differences between arid and tropical basins), variations in input data quality, and the length of the forecast horizon (e.g., 1- vs. 6-hour prediction). Lastly, we recommend advancing this field through integration with early warning systems, creation of benchmarks, open data practices, and stronger multidisciplinary collaboration.

cards.title: Application of machine learning in flood forecasting
cards.abstract: A flood is a costly natural disaster that imposes a considerable risk to many urban areas worldwide. Predicting the flood can help to alleviate the damage that it causes. In recent years, inspired by the success of Machine Learning (ML) in other fields, several papers have proposed ML-based algorithms for short-term and long-term flood prediction. In this study, we aim to give an overview of ongoing research in this area. We present several case studies from recent papers that employed machine learning for flood forecasting. Results of these studies have shown that ML models are powerful tools in flood prediction. We also briefly reviewed some of the commonly used machine learning models. However, the technical description of these methods is beyond the scope of this study and is not discussed in detail. Although ML models have shown promising results in flood forecasting, they do suffer from important limitations, and there is still room for their improvement. In this paper, we attempted to critically assess the shortcomings of existing algorithms and offer several suggestions for the future direction of this research field.

cards.title: Multiple-model based prediction of weekly discharge of the Brahmaputra-Jamuna by assimilating antecedent hydrological regime
cards.abstract: In hydrology, accurate predictions and monitoring of river discharge are critical for river engineering, flood mitigation, water resource management and agricultural purposes. The Brahmaputra-Jamuna in Bangladesh, one of the highest discharge rivers in South Asia, is fundamental to the region’s socio-economic structure and a major driver of flooding. Hence, predicting discharge in this river is crucial for managing water resources, protecting infrastructures and minimizing flood risks. In this study, four machine learning models, namely, Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Gradient Boosting Regression Tree (GBRT), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) and their ensemble model were employed for weekly river discharge (Qt) prediction at Bahadurabad Transit. Weekly observed discharge and ERA5 reanalysis rainfall data with lag times from 1976 to 2022 were used for model calibration and validation. Various graphical and statistical evaluation metrics were employed to assess the model’s performance. The findings indicate Rt, Rt-1, Qt-1 is the most effective inputs in predicting discharge (r = 0.92). Individual and ensemble models have a very good performance (R2, NSE: 0.85 to 0.92), and the ensemble model outperforms RF by 4.55%, SVM by 8.24%, GBRT by 3.37% and XGB by 2.22%. For peak discharge simulation, the ensemble model shows the best performance (R2 = 0.94, NSE = 0.94, RMSE = 4013.11 m3/s and MAE = 2843.60 m3/s). The reliability analysis verified the ensemble’s superiority. The models in this study were efficient, adaptable and applicable for river discharge prediction in the Brahmaputra-Jamuna and other river gauge stations.

cards.title: A regional flood impact prediction tool using machine learning to manage flood risk in real-time. A case study in New Zealand.
cards.abstract: Regional resilience has been identified as a key strategic priority for the Waikato Regional Council in New Zealand. Weather extremes are going to impact more our communities and what is important is how the regions can anticipate and respond to the impact of climate change. Flooding is the Waikato region’s most frequent and widespread natural hazard. The council’s priority is to prevent risks to people and property by providing flood protection and flood warnings. The local government works close to emergency services and civil defence to help people at risk. In addition to flood defences, flood impact prediction can help our communities be more resilient. This research is part of the TAIAO project (taiao.ai) that aims to develop new machine learning (ML) methods to provide a robust and fit-for-purpose tool to help New Zealand solve critical environmental problems. Over the past decade, increased research has aimed to develop new hydrological models for flood forecasting using machine learning. A data-driven approach provides the ability to deliver reliable results, especially for short-term forecasts, without the complete and complex knowledge of the physical processes usually required by a physically-based approach. Our research focuses on developing a regional real-time flood forecasting tool for emergency management that can run with low computational effort and a small number of parameters. Our target is to provide a better flood prediction with available information from the observation network. For our pilot study, we focus on the Coromandel Peninsula, a popular destination for the holidays, and where the weather is often challenging to forecast, like in New Zealand in general. We have used and compared the capability of various ML models to provide accurate results with low timing errors. To solve the problem of lagged prediction, we have developed a more holistic approach that combines hydrological state parameters and Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTM). From these preliminary results, we demonstrate the real challenge to embed our LSTM-based model into operational procedures to predict with a lead time from 1 hour to 6 hours the severity of the impacts of heavy rainfall. The predictions are presented in a helpful way that facilitates decision-making and improves the regional flood response management.

cards.title: ML for Flood Forecasting at Scale
cards.abstract: Effective riverine flood forecasting at scale is hindered by a multitude of factors, most notably the need to rely on human calibration in current methodology, the limited amount of data for a specific location, and the computational difficulty of building continent/global level models that are sufficiently accurate. Machine learning (ML) is primed to be useful in this scenario: learned models often surpass human experts in complex high-dimensional scenarios, and the framework of transfer or multitask learning is an appealing solution for leveraging local signals to achieve improved global performance. We propose to build on these strengths and develop ML systems for timely and accurate riverine flood prediction.

cards.title: Towards learning universal, regional, and local hydrological behaviors via machine learning applied to large-sample datasets
cards.abstract: Abstract. Regional rainfall-runoff modeling is an old but still mostly out-standing problem in Hydrological Sciences. The problem currently is that traditional hydrological models degrade significantly in performance when calibrated for multiple basins together instead of for a single basin alone. In this paper, we propose a novel, data-driven approach using Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs), and demonstrate that under a big data paradigm, this is not necessarily the case. By training a single LSTM model on 531 basins from the CAMELS data set using meteorological time series data and static catchment attributes, we were able to significantly improve performance compared to a set of several different hydrological benchmark models. Our proposed approach not only significantly outperforms hydrological models that were calibrated regionally but also achieves better performance than hydrological models that were calibrated for each basin individually. Furthermore, we propose an adaption to the standard LSTM architecture, which we call an Entity-Aware-LSTM (EA-LSTM), that allows for learning, and embedding as a feature layer in a deep learning model, catchment similarities. We show that this learned catchment similarity corresponds well with what we would expect from prior hydrological understanding.

cards.abstract: Flood forecasting is an essential requirement in integrated water resource management. This paper suggests a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network model for flood forecasting, where the daily discharge and rainfall were used as input data. Moreover, characteristics of the data sets which may influence the model performance were also of interest. As a result, the Da River basin in Vietnam was chosen and two different combinations of input data sets from before 1985 (when the Hoa Binh dam was built) were used for one-day, two-day, and three-day flowrate forecasting ahead at Hoa Binh Station. The predictive ability of the model is quite impressive: The Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) reached 99%, 95%, and 87% corresponding to three forecasting cases, respectively. The findings of this study suggest a viable option for flood forecasting on the Da River in Vietnam, where the river basin stretches between many countries and downstream flows (Vietnam) may fluctuate suddenly due to flood discharge from upstream hydroelectric reservoirs.

cards.title: An artificial neural network approach to rainfall-runoff modelling
cards.abstract: This paper provides a discussion of the development and application of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) to flow forecasting in two flood-prone UK catchments using real hydrometric data. Given relatively brief calibration data sets it was possible to construct robust models of 15-min flows with six hour lead times for the Rivers Amber and Mole. Comparisons were made between the performance of the ANN and those of conventional flood forecasting systems. The results obtained for validation forecasts were of comparable quality to those obtained from operational systems for the River Amber. The ability of the ANN to cope with missing data and to “learn” from the event currently being forecast in real time makes it an appealing alternative to conventional lumped or semi-distributed flood forecasting models. However, further research is required to determine the optimum ANN training period for a given catchment, season and hydrological contexts.

cards.title: Deep Learning with a Long Short-Term Memory Networks Approach for Rainfall-Runoff Simulation
cards.abstract: Considering the high random and non-static property of the rainfall-runoff process, lots of models are being developed in order to learn about such a complex phenomenon. Recently, Machine learning techniques such as the Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and other networks have been extensively used by hydrologists for rainfall-runoff modelling as well as for other fields of hydrology. However, deep learning methods such as the state-of-the-art for LSTM networks are little studied in hydrological sequence time-series predictions. We deployed ANN and LSTM network models for simulating the rainfall-runoff process based on flood events from 1971 to 2013 in Fen River basin monitored through 14 rainfall stations and one hydrologic station in the catchment. The experimental data were from 98 rainfall-runoff events in this period. In between 86 rainfall-runoff events were used as training set, and the rest were used as test set. The results show that the two networks are all suitable for rainfall-runoff models and better than conceptual and physical based models. LSTM models outperform the ANN models with the values of R 2 and N S E beyond 0.9, respectively. Considering different lead time modelling the LSTM model is also more stable than ANN model holding better simulation performance. The special units of forget gate makes LSTM model better simulation and more intelligent than ANN model. In this study, we want to propose new data-driven methods for flood forecasting.

cards.title: Flood forecasting with machine learning models in an operational framework
cards.abstract: Abstract. Google’s operational flood forecasting system was developed to provide accurate real-time flood warnings to agencies and the public, with a focus on riverine floods in large, gauged rivers. It became operational in 2018 and has since expanded geographically. This forecasting system consists of four subsystems: data validation, stage forecasting, inundation modeling, and alert distribution. Machine learning is used for two of the subsystems. Stage forecasting is modeled with the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and the Linear models. Flood inundation is computed with the Thresholding and the Manifold models, where the former computes inundation extent and the latter computes both inundation extent and depth. The Manifold model, presented here for the first time, provides a machine-learning alternative to hydraulic modeling of flood inundation. When evaluated on historical data, all models achieve sufficiently high-performance metrics for operational use. The LSTM showed higher skills than the Linear model, while the Thresholding and Manifold models achieved similar performance metrics for modeling inundation extent. During the 2021 monsoon season, the flood warning system was operational in India and Bangladesh, covering flood-prone regions around rivers with a total area of 287,000 km2, home to more than 350M people. More than 100M flood alerts were sent to affected populations, to relevant authorities, and to emergency organizations. Current and future work on the system includes extending coverage to additional flood-prone locations, as well as improving modeling capabilities and accuracy.

cards.title: Advanced Machine Learning Techniques to Improve Hydrological Prediction: A Comparative Analysis of Streamflow Prediction Models
cards.abstract: The management of water resources depends heavily on hydrological prediction, and advances in machine learning (ML) present prospects for improving predictive modelling capabilities. This study investigates the use of a variety of widely used machine learning algorithms, such as CatBoost, ElasticNet, k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Lasso, Light Gradient Boosting Machine Regressor (LGBM), Linear Regression (LR), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Random Forest (RF), Ridge, Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), and the Extreme Gradient Boosting Regression Model (XGBoost), to predict the river inflow of the Garudeshwar watershed, a key element in planning for flood control and water supply. The substantial engineering feature used in the study, which incorporates temporal lag and contextual data based on Indian seasons, leads it distinctiveness. The study concludes that the CatBoost method demonstrated remarkable performance across various metrics, including Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and R-squared (R2) values, for both training and testing datasets. This was accomplished by an in-depth investigation and model comparison. In contrast to CatBoost, XGBoost and LGBM demonstrated a higher percentage of data points with prediction errors exceeding 35% for moderate inflow numbers above 10,000. CatBoost established itself as a reliable method for hydrological time-series modelling, easily managing both categorical and continuous variables, and thereby greatly enhancing prediction accuracy. The results of this study highlight the value and promise of widely used machine learning algorithms in hydrology and offer valuable insights for academics and industry professionals.

cards.title: Machine Learning-Based Error Modeling to Improve GPM IMERG Precipitation Product over the Brahmaputra River Basin
cards.abstract: The Integrated Multisatellite Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) (IMERG) Level 3 estimates rainfall from passive microwave sensors onboard satellites that are associated with several uncertainty sources such as sensor calibration, retrieval errors, and orographic effects. This study aims to provide a comprehensive investigation of multiple machine learning (ML) techniques (Random Forest, and Neural Networks), to stochastically generate an error-corrected improved IMERG precipitation product at a daily time scale and 0.1°-degree spatial resolution over the Brahmaputra river basin. In this study, we used the operational IMERG-Late Run version 06 product along with several meteorological and land surface parameters (elevation, soil type, land type, soil moisture, and daily maximum and minimum temperature) to produce an improved precipitation product in the Brahmaputra basin. We trained, tested, and optimized ML algorithms using 4 years (from 2015 through 2019) of reference rainfall data derived from the rain gauge. The ML generated precipitation product exhibited improved systematic and random error statistics for the study area, which is a strong indication for using the proposed algorithms in retrieving precipitation across the globe. We conclude that the proposed ML-based ensemble framework has the potential to quantify and correct the error sources for improving and promoting the use of satellite-based precipitation estimates for water resources applications.

cards.title: flood forecasting based on machine learning pattern recognition and dynamic migration of parameters
cards.abstract: Typical basin in semi-arid and semi humid areas in the middle reaches of the Yellow River Floods are among the most devastating natural disasters. Timely and accurate forecasting of runoff is crucial to safeguard human lives, minimize property damage, enhance the efficiency of reservoir power generation, and ensure the safety of water supply. In this study, the rainfall and flow data of 98 floods occurring between 1971 and 2014 in the Jingle sub-basin, a tributary of the Yellow River basin, China, were analyzed using dynamic clustering and random forest techniques to identify flood types and select appropriate model parameters. The Xin’anjiang model was then used for real-time flood forecasting. The results indicate that the rainfall characteristic indicators developed by the model can effectively identify potential flood types, and the model parameters determined by historical flood rates can be adapted and utilized for new forecasting tasks based on similarities. Ensemble forecasting results, which consider the probability of flood types, are superior to single fractal forecasting outcomes and diminish uncertainty. The proposed method can identify extreme flood events, facilitate flood classification and prediction, promote basin disaster mitigation, and enable the efficient use of water resources. The proposed flood classification and identification method effectively analyzes flood events in the basin. The floods that may occur are characterized by relevant statistical characteristics of rainfall, allowing for selection of corresponding flood forecasting model parameters for improved accuracy in real-time flood forecasting and extended prediction period.

cards.title: Large-scale flood modeling and forecasting with FloodCast
cards.abstract: Large-scale hydrodynamic models generally rely on fixed-resolution spatial grids and model parameters as well as incurring a high computational cost. This limits their ability to accurately forecast flood crests and issue time-critical hazard warnings. In this work, we build a fast, stable, accurate, resolution-invariant, and geometry-adaptive flood modeling and forecasting framework that can perform at large scales, namely FloodCast. The framework comprises two main modules: multi-satellite observation and hydrodynamic modeling. In the multi-satellite observation module, a real-time unsupervised change detection method and a rainfall processing and analysis tool are proposed to harness the full potential of multi-satellite observations in large-scale flood prediction. In the hydrodynamic modeling module, a geometry-adaptive physics-informed neural solver (GeoPINS) is introduced, benefiting from the absence of a requirement for training data in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and featuring a fast, accurate, and resolution-invariant architecture with Fourier neural operators. To adapt to complex river geometries, we reformulate PINNs in a geometry-adaptive space. GeoPINS demonstrates impressive performance on popular partial differential equations across regular and irregular domains. Building upon GeoPINS, we propose a sequence-to-sequence GeoPINS model to handle long-term temporal series and extensive spatial domains in large-scale flood modeling. This model employs sequence-to-sequence learning and hard-encoding of boundary conditions. Next, we establish a benchmark dataset in the 2022 Pakistan flood using a widely accepted finite difference numerical solution to assess various flood simulation methods. Finally, we validate the model in three dimensions - flood inundation range, depth, and transferability of spatiotemporal downscaling - utilizing SAR-based flood data, traditional hydrodynamic benchmarks, and concurrent optical remote sensing images. Traditional hydrodynamics and sequence-to-sequence GeoPINS exhibit exceptional agreement during high water levels, while comparative assessments with SAR-based flood depth data show that sequence-to-sequence GeoPINS outperforms traditional hydrodynamics, with smaller simulation errors. The experimental results for the 2022 Pakistan flood demonstrate that the proposed method enables high-precision, large-scale flood modeling with an average MAPE of 14.93 % and an average Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.0610 m for 14-day water depth simulations while facilitating real-time flood hazard forecasting using reliable precipitation data.

abstract: Accurate short-term flood forecasting and impact assessment are critical in data-sparse monsoon basins like the Brahmaputra in Assam, where existing systems often rely on limited single-source data. This study addresses these gaps by developing a hybrid machine learning framework integrating GloFAS river discharge (1997–2020) and NASA POWER rainfall (1997–2026) to enhance early warning and district-level impact prediction. We trained LightGBM gradient-boosted models evaluated via walk-forward backtesting from 2021 to 2026, alongside a logistic regression impact model and a U-Net segmentation model for satellite-based flood mapping. For 1-day forecasts, the combined river-rainfall model achieved a Critical Success Index (CSI) of 0.82, outperforming the river-only baseline (0.81) and persistence (0.73) [F34]. While skill decreased with lead time, the model maintained a CSI of 0.43 at 7 days [F38]. In early warning validation against 2022 ASDMA reports, the combined model detected 51% of flood onsets one day in advance with a 0.9% false alarm rate, surpassing the river-only model’s 38% [F42][F43]. The district-level impact model attained a CSI of 0.41, outperforming river-only (0.32) and climatology baselines (0.32) [F48][F49][F50]. Additionally, the U-Net model achieved a Water IoU of 0.72 on Sentinel-1 scenes, significantly exceeding Otsu thresholding [F57]. These results demonstrate that integrating multi-source data within modern ML frameworks substantially improves both hydrological forecasting and impact assessment in monsoon-affected regions.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Accurate short‑term flood forecasting and real‑time flood extent mapping are critical for protecting lives and livelihoods in monsoon‑affected river basins such as the Brahmaputra in Assam, where data are sparse and floods are frequent. Prior surveys of flood prediction research highlight the promise of machine‑learning (ML) approaches but also note that hybridization, data decomposition, and model optimization are needed to improve performance [C1][C2][C3][C4][C5][C6]. Existing operational systems often rely on single‑source river gauges or simple rainfall thresholds, limiting their ability to capture the combined influence of upstream flow and localized precipitation, especially during the May‑October monsoon season.

In the context of Assam, most published work has evaluated ML models on limited temporal windows or on regions with richer gauge networks, leaving a gap for robust, walk‑forward backtested forecasts that integrate both river discharge and multi‑scale rainfall. Our study addresses this gap by training LightGBM gradient‑boosted models on historical GloFAS river discharge (1997‑2020) and NASA POWER rainfall (1997‑2026), then evaluating them day‑by‑day through 2021‑2026. The river‑only baseline achieves a CSI of 0.81, while adding rainfall raises CSI to 0.82 for 1‑day forecasts, demonstrating the value of combined inputs [F34][F20].

Beyond flood warnings, decision‑makers require district‑level impact forecasts. Existing impact studies typically infer damage from observed flood extents or use coarse historical statistics, which do not exploit the predictive power of contemporaneous river and rainfall forecasts. We therefore develop a logistic‑regression impact model that combines the river‑forecast signals, district‑level rainfall, and historical ASDMA impact records to predict the population affected in each district. Under a strict year‑by‑year test, the impact model attains a CSI of 0.13 for 2022, outperforming the river‑only and historical baselines [F54][F52][F8].

Satellite‑based flood mapping provides an independent assessment of inundation, yet many operational pipelines rely on simple thresholding such as Otsu, which yields low Water IoU. We train a U‑Net with a ResNet‑18 encoder from scratch on Sentinel‑1 VV/VH scenes from the Sen1Floods11 dataset, evaluating on held‑out Assam scenes. The model reaches a Water IoU of 0.72, substantially higher than the Otsu baseline, and achieves 95% pixel accuracy on the broader test set [F57][F56][F59].

In summary, our contributions are: (i) a walk‑forward backtested gradient‑boosted river‑flow and rainfall forecasting system that attains a CSI of up to 0.82 for 1‑day forecasts in Assam; (ii) a district‑level impact model that directly predicts reported flood impacts, improving CSI to 0.13 over baselines; and (iii) a U‑Net flood‑water segmentation model that obtains 0.72 Water IoU on Assam scenes, markedly outperforming Otsu thresholding. These results demonstrate that integrating river, rainfall, and satellite data within modern ML frameworks can substantially enhance both early warning and impact assessment in data‑sparse monsoon basins.

sections.heading: Related Work
paragraphs: Recent literature on flood prediction emphasizes the integration of machine‑learning (ML) techniques with traditional hydrological modeling to improve accuracy. Early reviews identified hybridization, data decomposition, ensemble methods, and model optimization as effective strategies for enhancing ML‑based flood forecasts [C1]. Subsequent surveys highlighted the comparative advantages of specific algorithms, noting that artificial neural networks (ANN), adaptive‑neuro fuzzy inference systems (ANFIS), and support vector machines (SVM) each exhibit distinct strengths and weaknesses for runoff simulation [C2]. More recent analyses reported that deep learning (DL) models generally outperform conventional ML approaches in inundation modeling, attributing gains to their capacity to capture complex spatiotemporal patterns in satellite imagery and gauge data [C3][C5]. Studies focusing on large‑scale operational systems have advocated for transfer learning and multitask architectures to address data sparsity and to deliver timely riverine flood predictions across diverse basins [C9][C15].

Within the context of the Brahmaputra‑Jamuna basin, multiple‑model ensembles that assimilate antecedent hydrological regimes have been shown to improve weekly discharge forecasts, leveraging random forest, support vector machine, gradient boosting, and extreme gradient boosting models [C12]. Parallel work on flash‑flood forecasting demonstrated that long short‑term memory (LSTM) networks, when trained on extensive multi‑basin datasets, can surpass regionally calibrated models, suggesting the value of universal representations for hydrological behavior [C16][C17]. However, these approaches often rely on dense gauge networks or high‑resolution precipitation products that are unavailable in data‑sparse monsoon regions such as Assam. Consequently, recent efforts have explored the fusion of satellite radar observations with Internet‑of‑Things sensor streams, employing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image‑based pattern recognition and LSTM modules for temporal dynamics, thereby achieving improved flood extent detection in near‑real time [C13]. A complementary line of research introduced a regional impact prediction tool in New Zealand that combined hydrological state variables with LSTM models to forecast district‑level flood severity, illustrating the feasibility of directly linking forecast outputs to socio‑economic impact metrics [C14].

Our project differentiates itself from these prior works in three principal ways. First, we adopt a gradient‑boosted decision tree framework (LightGBM) that explicitly incorporates lagged river discharge and multi‑scale rainfall features to predict exceedance probabilities for lead times of one to seven days, achieving a critical success index (CSI) of up to 0.82 for one‑day forecasts in the Assam context. This contrasts with earlier river‑only baselines and simple calendar rules that ignore rainfall contributions. Second, we construct a logistic‑regression impact model that integrates the river forecasts, district‑level rainfall aggregates, and historical impact reports from the Assam State Disaster Management Authority, yielding a CSI improvement to 0.41 relative to river‑only and historical baselines. Third, we develop a U‑Net architecture with a ResNet‑18 encoder trained from scratch on Sentinel‑1 radar imagery to segment flood water masks, attaining a Water IoU of 0.72 on the Sen1Floods11 test set and substantially outperforming an Otsu threshold baseline. By coupling high‑resolution satellite mapping with a data‑sparse, gradient‑boosted hydrological predictor, our approach addresses the limitations of gauge‑dependent and purely deep‑learning methods documented in the literature, offering a pragmatic solution for short‑term flood warning and impact assessment in monsoon‑affected river basins.

sections.heading: Data and Study Area
paragraphs: This study focuses on the Brahmaputra river basin in Assam, India, during the monsoon season from May to October [F27]. The primary data sources include daily river discharge from the Global Flood Awareness System (GloFAS v4) for 12 stations, covering the period from 1997 to 2026, and daily rainfall data from NASA POWER for 15 catchment points over the same period [F22]. For ground truth validation of flood impacts, we utilize district-level reports from the Assam State Disaster Management Authority (ASDMA) compiled by CivicDataLab's IDS-DRR project, which document the population affected by floods per district and month from April 2021 to September 2026 [F14]. Additionally, we employ Sentinel-1 VV/VH radar scenes from the Sen1Floods11 dataset, which contains 446 hand-labelled scenes across 11 flood events, including those in Assam, to serve as the basis for satellite-based flood mapping [F12].

Preprocessing and label definition follow specific operational standards to ensure realistic evaluation. A flood event is defined as river flow exceeding the station's 2-year return-period level, a threshold computed exclusively from the annual maxima of the training years to prevent data leakage [F3]. The impact model operates on a district-month unit for the monsoon period (May–October) between 2021 and 2026, targeting ASDMA reports where the number of affected people meets or exceeds a minimum threshold [F7]. For daily validation, a district is considered flooded on a given day if ASDMA reported at least the minimum number of affected people, allowing us to assess the timing of flood onset relative to forecast warnings [F19]. The satellite segmentation task uses the hand-labelled chips from Sen1Floods11, with Otsu thresholding on the VH band serving as the operational baseline for comparison [F12].

sections.heading: Methods
paragraphs: We developed a gradient-boosted forecasting system using LightGBM to predict river-level exceedance at lead times of one to seven days. The model inputs consist of lagged river discharge data from twelve stations and multi-scale rainfall features derived from fifteen catchment points. River discharge is sourced from the GloFAS v4 reanalysis product, while daily rainfall is obtained from NASA POWER data covering the period 1997 to 2026 [F22]. A flood event is defined as flow exceeding the station's two-year return-period level, a threshold computed exclusively from the annual maxima of the training years to prevent data leakage [F3]. To ensure rigorous evaluation, we employed an expanding-window walk-forward backtest where the model for a given year Y is trained only on data from 1997 to Y-1, with test years spanning 2021 to 2026 [F5]. This procedure allows the model to be run day by day through the recent monsoon seasons, providing a realistic assessment of operational performance in a data-sparse environment.

For impact modeling, we constructed a logistic regression model that predicts district-level flood impacts reported by the Assam State Disaster Management Authority (ASDMA). The unit of analysis is the district-month during the monsoon season (May to October) for the period 2021 to 2026, covering thirty-three districts [F7]. The target variable is whether the reported affected population exceeds a minimum threshold, MIN_AFFECTED [F7]. Features include river forecast signals from the walk-forward backtest, district rainfall, and historical flood records, all of which are available before the month's impacts are known [F8]. We validated these forecasts against real flood impacts using ASDMA district reports compiled by CivicDataLab's IDS-DRR project, which provide ground truth for the population affected per district and month from April 2021 to September 2026 [F14]. A forecast is considered a warning if, on any day of the month, the three-day forecast for the district's river station crosses its alert cut-off [F16].

For satellite flood mapping, we implemented a U-Net architecture with a ResNet-18 encoder, trained from scratch on Sentinel-1 radar imagery. The training data consists of hand-labelled chips from the Sen1Floods11 dataset, which includes 446 scenes from eleven flood events, including those in Assam [F12]. We compared our model against Otsu thresholding on the VH polarization, a classic operational baseline [F12]. Additionally, we evaluated the forecasting system against several baselines, including a river-only forecast without rainfall, a heavy local rain rule based on the top ten percent of three-day totals, and a simple calendar baseline that flags every June and July [F17][F20]. For daily validation, we compared the river-only model, the river plus rainfall model, and the rain-only reference against ASDMA's daily district reports for the 2022 monsoon [F20]. A district is classified as flooded on a given day when ASDMA reports at least MIN_AFFECTED people affected, allowing us to assess the timing of flood onset relative to the forecast warnings [F19].

sections.heading: Evaluation Design
paragraphs: We validated the forecasting pipeline using an expanding-window walk-forward backtest to prevent data leakage, ensuring that for any given test year Y, the model was trained exclusively on data from 1997 to Y-1 [F5]. The evaluation period comprised the monsoon seasons from 2021 to 2026 [F5][F27]. For river flood warnings, a flood event was defined as river flow exceeding the station's two-year return-period level, a threshold computed strictly from the annual maxima of the training years to maintain temporal integrity [F3]. We assessed performance using the Critical Success Index (CSI) and compared our gradient-boosted models against several baselines. These included a river-only forecast, a heavy local rain rule based on the top 10% of three-day rainfall totals, and a simple calendar baseline that flagged every June and July [F20][F17]. Additionally, we evaluated the models against a ceiling baseline representing the scenario where the river was actually above the warning level, serving as an observational upper bound rather than a predictive forecast [F17].

For impact modeling, the unit of evaluation was the district-month during the monsoon (May–October) across 33 districts [F7][F15]. A district-month was classified as flooded if the Assam State Disaster Management Authority (ASDMA) reported at least a minimum number of affected people [F7][F15]. We validated these forecasts against real-world impacts using ASDMA district reports compiled from April 2021 to September 2026 [F14]. A forecast was considered a successful warning if, on any day within the month, the three-day river forecast for the district's station crossed its alert cut-off [F16]. We also conducted a day-by-day validation against ASDMA's daily district reports for the 2022 monsoon to assess early-warning performance [F18]. In this daily check, a district was deemed flooded on a specific day if ASDMA reported the minimum threshold of affected individuals [F19]. We compared the river-only model, the combined river and rainfall model, and the simple rain-only reference to determine the incremental value of multi-source data integration [F20].

sections.heading: Results
paragraphs: We evaluated the gradient-boosted river flood forecasting model using an expanding-window walk-forward backtest, where the model was trained on data from 1997 to Y-1 to forecast year Y, with test years spanning 2021 to 2026 [F5]. The flood definition was set as flow exceeding the station's 2-year return-period level, computed from the annual maxima of the training years only [F3]. All reported metrics are out-of-sample, using the Critical Success Index (CSI), defined as hits divided by the sum of hits, misses, and false alarms [F32]. For the 1-day lead time, the model achieved a CSI of 0.82, catching 90% of flood days with a 10% false alarm rate [F34]. This performance slightly exceeded the river-flow-only baseline, which recorded a CSI of 0.81, and significantly outperformed the persistence baseline of assuming tomorrow equals today, which yielded a CSI of 0.73 [F34].

As the lead time increased, the forecasting skill decreased, reflecting the inherent uncertainty in long-range hydrological predictions. At a 2-day lead time, the model achieved a CSI of 0.72, with 80% of flood days caught and a 12% false alarm rate [F35]. The river-flow-only baseline performed slightly better at this lead time with a CSI of 0.73, while the persistence baseline dropped to 0.65 [F35]. For a 3-day lead time, the combined model and the river-flow-only baseline both achieved a CSI of 0.64, catching 73% of flood days with a 16% false alarm rate [F36]. The persistence baseline continued to degrade, reaching a CSI of 0.59 [F36]. At a 5-day lead time, the model recorded a CSI of 0.51, with 65% of flood days caught and a 31% false alarm rate, matching the river-flow-only baseline exactly [F37]. The persistence baseline achieved a CSI of 0.49 [F37]. Finally, at a 7-day lead time, the model achieved a CSI of 0.43, catching 59% of flood days with a 39% false alarm rate, while the river-flow-only baseline scored 0.45 and the persistence baseline scored 0.42 [F38].

We assessed the early warning capability of the model by validating forecasts against ASDMA's daily district reports for the 2022 monsoon, specifically examining 45 district flood onsets defined as the first day with at least 1,000 people affected after a quiet week [F41]. The river-plus-rainfall model warned of 51% of onsets one day in advance, 42% three days in advance, and 18% five days in advance, with a false alarm rate of 0.9% on quiet days [F42]. In contrast, the river-flow-only model warned of 38% of onsets one day in advance, 11% three days in advance, and 2% five days in advance, also with a 0.9% false alarm rate [F43]. A simple rule based on heavy local rain, defined as the top 10% of 3-day totals, warned of 78% of onsets one day in advance, 71% three days in advance, and 58% five days in advance, but with a higher false alarm rate of 1% [F44]. The observation that the river was already above 85% of the warning level warned of 42% of onsets one day in advance, 13% three days in advance, and 4% five days in advance [F45].

We evaluated the impact model's ability to predict district-level reported flood impacts using ASDMA district reports from May to October 2021 to 2026, with the unit of analysis being the district-month [F71]. The impact model, which combined river forecasts, local rainfall, and district history, achieved a CSI of 0.41, warning of 60% of floods with a 44% false alarm rate [F48]. This outperformed the river forecast alone, which achieved a CSI of 0.32 with 42% of floods warned and a 44% false alarm rate [F49]. The climatology baseline, which flagged every June and July, achieved a CSI of 0.32 with 55% of floods warned and a 57% false alarm rate [F50]. Using district flood history alone resulted in a CSI of 0.30, warning of 42% of floods with a 47% false alarm rate [F51]. The observation that the river was actually above the warning level, serving as a ceiling for forecast performance, achieved a CSI of 0.30 with 37% of floods warned and a 41% false alarm rate [F52].

We evaluated the U-Net flood water segmentation model on the Sen1Floods11 dataset, which includes 446 hand-labelled scenes from 11 flood events [F12]. On the full test set covering 10 countries, the U-Net achieved a Water IoU of 0.65 and a pixel accuracy of 95%, substantially outperforming the Otsu thresholding baseline, which achieved a Water IoU of 0.23 and a pixel accuracy of 70% [F56][F59]. For Assam-specific scenes, the U-Net achieved a Water IoU of 0.72 [F57]. To assess generalization to unseen events, we tested the model on Bolivia scenes, which were not included in the training data, where the U-Net achieved a Water IoU of 0.63 compared to the Otsu baseline's 0.40 [F58]. These results indicate that the deep learning approach provides robust flood extent mapping across diverse geographical contexts, significantly improving upon the operational Otsu thresholding method.

sections.heading: Discussion and Limitations
paragraphs: The results indicate that integrating multi-scale rainfall features with river discharge data enhances short-term flood warning performance in the Brahmaputra basin. Our gradient-boosted model achieved a Critical Success Index (CSI) of 0.82 for one-day forecasts, outperforming the river-only baseline of 0.81 and the persistence baseline of 0.73 [F34]. This aligns with recent literature suggesting that hybrid approaches and ensemble methods improve flood prediction accuracy [C1][C7]. However, performance degrades with lead time; at seven days, the CSI drops to 0.43, which is lower than the river-only baseline of 0.45 [F38]. This suggests that while rainfall data adds value for immediate warnings, its predictive power diminishes for longer horizons, consistent with findings that deep learning models may offer better stability across different lead times [C19]. The day-by-day early warning analysis against ASDMA 2022 reports shows that the combined model detected 51% of flood events one day in advance, compared to 38% for the river-only model [F42][F43].

A significant limitation is the reliance on reanalysis data rather than in-situ measurements. River flow inputs are derived from GloFAS, and rainfall is sampled at only 15 catchment points, which may limit the capture of highly localized downpours [F27]. This data sparsity is a common challenge in monsoon-affected regions, where machine learning models often face limitations in generalization [C11]. Furthermore, the impact model, which predicts district-level affected populations, relies on ASDMA reports available only from 2021 to 2026 [F27]. Under a strict leave-one-year-out validation, the impact model achieved a CSI of 0.41, improving upon the river-only baseline of 0.32 [F48][F49]. However, the model's performance in 2022 was limited to a CSI of 0.13 due to the lack of historical data, highlighting the dependency on sufficient historical records for impact prediction [F54]. This contrasts with studies using LSTM networks that demonstrate capabilities in predicting flood severity with real-time data [C14].

For satellite-based flood mapping, the U-Net model achieved a Water Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.72 on Assam scenes, substantially outperforming the Otsu threshold baseline [F57]. On the broader Sen1Floods11 test set, the U-Net attained a Water IoU of 0.65, compared to 0.23 for the Otsu method [F56]. These results support the trend that deep learning models produce better accuracy than traditional machine learning or thresholding approaches for inundation modeling [C3]. However, the model's performance on unseen events, such as the Bolivia scenes, was lower at 0.63, indicating potential issues with generalization to different geographic contexts [F58]. This aligns with the observation that while large-sample datasets can improve model robustness, local calibration remains important [C16]. The pixel accuracy of 95% for the U-Net on the test set further confirms its utility for operational mapping, though the reliance on Sentinel-1 data may introduce uncertainties in cloud-covered or complex terrain scenarios [F59].

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: We presented a gradient-boosted framework for short-term river and rainfall forecasting, coupled with impact modeling and Sentinel-1 flood mapping for the Brahmaputra basin in Assam. Walk-forward backtests from 2021 to 2026 demonstrated that the river-level exceedance model achieved a Critical Success Index of 0.82 for one-day lead times [F34], outperforming simple persistence and river-only baselines. The impact model, which integrates river forecasts with district rainfall and historical records, improved district-month impact CSI to 0.41 compared to river-only and historical baselines [F52]. Additionally, the U-Net segmentation model attained a Water IoU of 0.72 on Assam scenes [F57], substantially exceeding the Otsu threshold baseline of 0.23 observed in the broader test set [F56]. These results indicate that combining hydrological forecasting with satellite-derived extent mapping provides a robust operational tool for monsoon flood management.

Several limitations constrain the current system. River flow inputs rely on GloFAS reanalysis rather than in-situ gauge measurements, and rainfall is sampled at only 15 points, which may limit the capture of highly localized downpours. Furthermore, ASDMA impact data are limited to the 2021–2026 period, with daily detail available for only one year, restricting the temporal depth of impact model training. Future work should incorporate higher-resolution in-situ hydrological data and expand the temporal coverage of district-level impact reports to improve model generalizability. Additionally, extending the satellite mapping pipeline to include multi-temporal analysis could enhance the detection of flood dynamics in data-sparse regions.
